I think audiences expect very different things from the stage than they do from TV or film. What you see and how you see it are differently constructed, which affects how audiences react. Also, I think this particular scene would probably have gone over very differently if it was 'straight theatre' rather than opera.

In the UK, because we used to have quite strict censorship of theatre, artists have tended to intentionally challenge that, and there's always been a sector of the arts that is purposefully avant-garde. This applies to ballet and opera too, of course, right back to Ballet Russes, although I think all three forms do operate very differently.

Sure, there's still a view of opera as stuffy, and maybe it's tempting to just say "elitist audiences at the Royal Opera House don't expect this material in their traditionalist entertainment", but I think that wouldn't necessarily be true, because opera and ballet can be and frequently are very modernist media (thinking people like Balletboyz, who are often quite raw and sexual, or at least sensual, in performance). However, opera particularly has strong traditions of parsing sex and violence in certain ways. It's an art form that's about exaggeration of emotion and concept, but that relies on implication. It's not inherently realistic, or naturalistic.

In the case of this specific production, most of the negative reviews and reactions seem to be accusations of sensationalism - people felt the scene was unnecessary and went on too long. Without having seen it myself, I couldn't comment on how well I think it served its purpose in the production, but the basic idea - taking a scene where, in the original libretto (AFAIK), the Swiss women are made to dance for the Austrian soldiers (which surely already implies the distinct possibility of rape/violation/assault happening too) and making it into a graphic depiction of actual rape - does run the risk of being seen as done for shock value and nothing more... and that's an accusation that gets levelled at TV and movies, too.
